19156.text: W Pottawattamie County carried $75.9 million in crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2012, with heat and drought as the largest cause at 45 percent of that total. That share rose from 8 percent in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2000-2009 to 56 percent in 2010-2019. The loss ratio over the last ten crop years measured was 1.06, with 6 of 19 crop years paying out more than premium collected. Irrigation failure indemnities stood at $0.02 million across all years, and no renewable energy capacity is operating or proposed.

27112.text: West Otter Tail County paid out 39.3 million dollars in crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2012, with excess moisture and flood accounting for 32 percent of losses. The loss ratio over that period was 0.46, meaning the county returned less in indemnities than it paid in premiums, and only 2 of 18 crop years paid out more than premium. Heat and drought's share of indemnities rose from 11 percent in the 1989–1999 period to 34 percent in 2000–2009, then held at 30 percent in 2010–2019. Cash rent and corn yield are withheld.

27120.text: West Polk County drew $146.9 million in crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2012, with excess moisture and flood accounting for 49 percent of that total. The loss ratio over the last ten crop years measured 0.29, with 7 of 24 years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought share of indemnities rose from 4 percent in 1989–1999 to 12 percent in 2000–2009 and held at 12 percent through 2010–2019. Cash rent and corn yield are withheld. Night heat and water dependence are not yet measured.

01001.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Autauga County sits at 50.5 dollars per acre in 2026, up 50.7 percent from 2016. Land value reached 2636 dollars per acre in 2022, rising 19.5 percent over 2017-2022, with rent running at 1.93 percent of that value. Crop insurance indemnities totaled 10.1 million dollars over 1989-2025, with heat and drought accounting for 55 percent; the loss ratio over 2017-2026 stands at 0.51. Irrigation covers 6 percent of harvested cropland, drawn entirely from groundwater, and corn yield is withheld.

01003.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Baldwin County sits at 90 dollars per acre in 2026, up 27.7 percent from 2016. The irrigated premium runs 53 dollars per acre with no clear direction of change. Corn yields trended upward at 3.112 bushels per acre per year over 2009-2025, though the worst year, 2011, fell to 65.9 bushels per acre. The crop insurance loss ratio reached 0.78 over 2017-2026, and excess moisture and flood drove 37 percent of the 52.4 million dollars in indemnities paid out across 1989-2026, while heat and drought accounted for 22 percent in 2020-2026.

01005.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Barbour County stands at 58.5 dollars per acre in 2026, up 69.6 percent from 2016. The crop insurance loss ratio for 2017-2026 is 0.6, meaning recent premiums have exceeded indemnities paid out. Corn yields carry a fitted trend of 5.526 bushels per acre per year across 2009-2023, with a median of 166.3 bushels per acre, though the worst year on record in that span, 2010, fell to 79.4. Heat and drought drove 75 percent of the 40 million dollars in total indemnities during 2000-2009, and that cause has remained the leading one across every period measured through 2026.

01007.text: Non-irrigated cash rent in Bibb County, AL stands at 24 dollars per acre in 2026, up 140 percent from 2014. Census land value was 2,611 dollars per acre in 2022, though that figure moved down 7 percent over 2017-2022. The rent-to-value ratio sits at 0.57 percent.
